meta.title: Split a box until the pieces are small enough
meta.description: RECURSIVE SUBDIVISION AS A ONE-RULE GRAMMAR. A split grammar is normally a function that calls itself on each half; here it is `applyRules` with a single rule, `cell`, and a graph with no cycle in it. Each round the wrapper feeds every cell labelled `cell` to the rule, and the rule does two things: it RELABELS the cells that are small enough to `panel`, a label with no rule, so they leave on `out` and are never fed again; and it HALVES the rest with `splitBox`, labelling both halves `cell` so the next round feeds them back. What comes out is the leaves -- the panels -- and that is what a facade needs. A CELL IS A POINT, and the box it stands for is the `boundsMin`/`boundsMax` pair every point already carries: `rootCell` writes the 24 x 15 x 0.4 panel on one point, and every split writes boxes on new points without moving them. THE CUT GOES ACROSS THE LONGEST SPAN: `axis` "longest" with `longestOf` "xy", the plane of the wall, so the depth is never a candidate. Splitting the longest span is what keeps the cells from degenerating into slivers -- cut a fixed axis and every cell ends up as tall as the facade and a finger wide -- and a square cell, where the two tie, is cut along x. WHERE TO CUT IS THE PARENT'S DECISION, and the node makes it impossible to get wrong. The cut fraction is a share of the cell in [0.34, 0.66), drawn from `ruleRoll` -- the number in [0, 1) applyRules writes on every cell it feeds -- and written as the relative `sizes` vec(f, 1 - f). `splitBox` resolves `sizes` ONCE per cell, on the PARENT, before it cuts, so both halves meet at one f32 coordinate. A fraction drawn on each child after the cut would land at two different coordinates and leave a strip that belongs to neither half or to both, with every cell still a valid box and the picture still a subdivided panel; there is no place in this rule to write that, because nothing runs between the draw and the cut. The leaves tile the root exactly -- summed area 360 against a root of 360, at every seed from 0 to 199 -- which is the assertion worth making about a subdivision and the one a picture cannot make for you. THE STOP RULE IS THE RELABEL, and it is the only thing in the rule that is about this facade: a cell becomes a `panel` once its longest span is 1.7 or less, or once it is nine splits deep (`ruleDepth`, the round the wrapper writes, is the number of splits behind a cell). The size floor alone would end it -- each half keeps at most 66% of the span it was cut from, so the longest span shrinks geometrically. The depth cap is a choice about the picture, not a guard against running forever: over seeds 0 to 199 it binds in 198, stopping about nine cells per facade (at most 19) while their longest span is still above 1.7, so the finest corners stop a split or two early. A depth cap alone would not do instead: it leaves the cells of a wide facade still wide. EVERY RELABEL COSTS A ROUND: a panel settles one round after the split that made it, so on `out` its `ruleDepth` is one more than its split count, and `maxDepth` 12 leaves room above the cap's ten rounds. WHAT IT IS NOT: a facade with a vocabulary. Every cell splits by the same rule, so this makes a Mondrian; `basics-apply-rules` is the same recursion as one rule among several -- facades, floors, panels, windows -- each with its own label. The four nodes after the grammar only draw the panels: a unit box copied onto every leaf, centred on its box and scaled to 86% of it so the joints show.
